title: Warring States China
capsule: The Warring States period (traditionally 475–221 BCE) saw seven major states — Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Wei, and Zhao — wage near-continuous warfare while undertaking radical administrative and military reforms that transformed the Zhou feudal order into a system of bureaucratic, conscript-army kingdoms. Legalist statecraft, exemplified by Shang Yang's reforms in Qin from 356 BCE onward, gave Qin a structural advantage in mobilizing agriculture and warfare; Qin's conquests of Han (230), Zhao (228), Wei (225), Chu (223), Yan (222), and Qi (221) completed unification under Qin Shi Huang, who declared himself the first emperor. The period also produced the major texts of Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism, and the Hundred Schools of Thought.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. State territories are documented through the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) and Zhanguo Ce, but precise inter-state borders shifted constantly with military fortunes and are approximated in modern scholarship.
